title: AI safety in national security
summary: The US military and intelligence community are integrating AI into some of the highest-stakes decisions in the world, but few people focused on AI safety work there. Learn whether a career in US national security is right for you, and how to get in.
body_markdown:
## Summary


**In a nutshell:** Some of the most consequential (and potentially most dangerous) uses of AI are in national security: autonomous weapons, cyber capabilities, and intelligence analysis that feeds decisions about the use of force. Few people focused on AI safety work in this field, and the US government’s defense spending gives it substantial influence over what AI companies build. Working in national security could put you in a position to reduce some of the most serious risks from AI. At the same time, entry is slow, much of the work is classified, and there’s a serious risk of contributing to harm.


**Pros:**


- Some of the most consequential uses of AI — autonomous weapons, AI-enabled cyberattacks, and AI-driven intelligence analysis — are being deployed by national security institutions.
- Government spending shapes what AI companies build, so people inside the national security establishment can push for (or against) specific safety features.
- Relatively few people in these institutions are knowledgeable about the full range of risks from advanced AI, so that expertise can be especially valuable here.


**Cons:**


- These roles carry a real risk of doing harm, including by lending legitimacy to dangerous AI deployments.
- Much of the work is classified, which makes it harder to get an outside perspective on your choices.
- You may not work with anyone else who is primarily motivated by AI safety.


**Key facts on fit:**


- Most government roles require US citizenship and many require a security clearance. Most jobs also require living in or near DC, or a regional hub for your agency.
- Many roles need less technical skill than you might expect. Social skills, clear writing, and the ability to brief busy people often matter more.
- You’ll need to be comfortable working alongside the military and serving US interests specifically.
